Newly emerged hatchlings of Iberolacerta aurelioi are remarkably small, with a snout–vent length of 2.76 cm [Lb = 2.76 cm] at the moment of egg tooth action and initial shell pipping. This diminutive size is typical of lacertid lizards that exploit high-elevation rocky habitats. The wet weight at birth is similarly modest at 0.43 g [Wwb = 0.43 g], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo within the parchment-shelled egg. When eggs are incubated at a stable 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a thermal regime that mimics the warmest crevice microsites on sun-exposed talus slopes, the incubation period lasts 35.6 days [ab = 35.6 days] before the neonate emerges. This duration is intermediate among European rock lizards, balancing the opposing pressures of rapid development in a short alpine summer against the need for adequate yolk absorption to support a fully formed juvenile.

Following the onset of exogenous feeding, juveniles of I. aurelioi enter a period of rapid somatic growth that continues until reproductive maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity in females is marked by the pubertal snout–vent length of 4.84 cm [Lp = 4.84 cm], a size that typically requires several seasons of active feeding to achieve. For males, the pubertal snout–vent length is slightly smaller, recorded at 4.51 cm [Lp = 4.51 cm], a sexually dimorphic pattern that contrasts with the ultimate adult sizes. The time since birth at which females reach this pubertal milestone, under the cool thermal conditions of their montane environment, is approximately 4.5 years [tp = approximately 4.5 years], a value measured at the mean annual temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] typical of their subalpine habitat. Males, maturing at a slightly smaller body size, reach puberty at a comparable time since birth of 4.5 years [tp = 4.5 years] under the same 14 °C [T = 14 °C] thermal regime. This late maturation is characteristic of high-altitude lacertids and reflects the constraints of a short growing season.

The ultimate body size attained by reproductively active adults of I. aurelioi shows a clear sexual dimorphism that aligns with the species' life-history strategy. Adult females reach a maximum snout–vent length of 6.22 cm [Li = 6.22 cm], a size that optimises the volume of the body cavity available for carrying a clutch of eggs. In contrast, adult males achieve a slightly larger ultimate snout–vent length of 6.53 cm [Li = 6.53 cm], a difference that is modest in absolute terms but consistent with the pattern of male-male competition for territories on rocky outcrops. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for both sexes combined is 5.12 g [Wwi = 5.12 g], a mass that is relatively light compared to that of lowland lacertids, likely an adaptation for agile climbing on vertical rock faces. Field-captured gravid females often approach this maximum mass as they carry fully yolked eggs, underscoring the physiological demands of reproduction at altitude.

Longevity in the wild for I. aurelioi is constrained by the harsh environmental conditions of its alpine home as well as the metabolic costs of surviving multiple winters. The maximum lifespan, recorded at a mean ambient temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], is approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years], a value derived from mark-recapture studies of individually marked lizards on stable talus slopes. This is a remarkably long lifespan for a small lacertid, exceeding that of most lowland congeners by several years. The cool thermal regime likely slows the intrinsic rate of senescence, as reduced metabolic rates at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] minimise oxidative damage over time. The oldest individuals are typically males that have held prime territories for over a decade, indicating that territorial tenure is a major predictor of survival in this species.

Beyond the life-history metrics directly linked to development and reproduction, the ecology of I. aurelioi is intimately tied to the thermal properties of its preferred microhabitat. The species is an obligate heliotherm, relying on basking to elevate its body temperature above the ambient 14 °C [T = 14 °C] that defines the average conditions near its rock crevices. Gravid females, in particular, select the warmest available basking sites to accelerate embryonic development, although the fundamental incubation temperature for successful hatching is 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a value that is rarely sustained for long periods in the field. The combination of a long lifespan, which far exceeds that of lowland lacertids rarely surviving beyond five years, and a late age at first reproduction means that population turnover is exceptionally slow. This demographic pattern makes the species particularly vulnerable to habitat disturbance, as the removal of even a few reproductively mature adults can take decades to compensate through natural recruitment.
